title: Track and Field: training overview
d: Track and Field training builds the fitness, skills, and tactics the rules demand.
definition: Track and Field training builds the fitness, skills, and tactics the rules demand.
description: Track and Field training has three pillars: the physical engine, the technical skills, and the tactical brain. The rules define the demands — individual over meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes — and training reverses them into a program: energy systems for the duration, strength for the collisions and jumps, skills for the techniques, tactics for the decisions. This database covers all four across a season, from first preseason week to championship taper.

facts.duration: meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes

title: Energy systems
d: Track and Field runs on: Field-team sports are built on repeated high-intensity efforts over meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes. Aerobic base plus sprint repeatability decides the fourth quarter..
definition: Track and Field runs on: Field-team sports are built on repeated high-intensity efforts over meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes. Aerobic base plus sprint repeatability decides the fourth quarter..
description: Energy-system training for Track and Field: Field-team sports are built on repeated high-intensity efforts over meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes. Aerobic base plus sprint repeatability decides the fourth quarter. Match the conditioning to the clock — train the exact work-to-rest ratios the sport uses, because fitness is specific. Test the systems with time trials and heart-rate data, then target the weakest one first; the fittest athlete is rarely the winner, but the unfittest never is.

title: Strength program
d: Track and Field strength work: Lower-body power and single-leg strength: squats, lunges, and plyometrics transfer directly to sprinting and tackling..
definition: Track and Field strength work: Lower-body power and single-leg strength: squats, lunges, and plyometrics transfer directly to sprinting and tackling..
description: Strength training for Track and Field: Lower-body power and single-leg strength: squats, lunges, and plyometrics transfer directly to sprinting and tackling. Train strength twice a week in season, three times out of it. Lift for the sport, not for the mirror — every exercise should answer which on-field action it improves. Keep a training log; progressive overload over months is what separates good from great.

title: Conditioning plan
d: Track and Field conditioning mirrors meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes: work-to-rest matched to the game clock.
definition: Track and Field conditioning mirrors meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes: work-to-rest matched to the game clock.
description: Conditioning for Track and Field must mirror the game clock: meets run hours; events seconds to ~30 minutes. Build the aerobic base first — it speeds recovery between hard efforts — then layer sport-specific intervals. Never sacrifice skill sessions for extra running; tired athletes learn bad technique. Monitor with resting heart rate and repeat-sprint tests.

title: Skill acquisition
d: Learn Track and Field skills in three stages: grooved, pressured, then match-random.
definition: Learn Track and Field skills in three stages: grooved, pressured, then match-random.
description: Skill learning in Track and Field follows blocked-to-random progression: first groove the movement alone, then add pressure, then randomize like a match. Ten thousand mindless reps engrave errors; one thousand deliberate reps with feedback engrave skill. Film everything — athletes cannot fix what they cannot see.

title: Tactical training
d: Track and Field tactics are rehearsed, not improvised: walk, jog, full speed, then live.
definition: Track and Field tactics are rehearsed, not improvised: walk, jog, full speed, then live.
description: Tactical training in Track and Field: walk through the shape, jog it, run it full speed, then go live. Tactics fail when players think instead of recognize — so rehearse until recognition is instant. Review film weekly: pause at decisions and ask what the right choice was before revealing it.

facts.objective: finish first, jump or throw farthest/highest

title: Sports nutrition
d: Fuel Track and Field: carbs for the work, protein for repair, timing around sessions.
definition: Fuel Track and Field: carbs for the work, protein for repair, timing around sessions.
description: Nutrition for Track and Field athletes: carbohydrate covers the training load, protein (about 1.6-2.2 g per kg daily) repairs it, and fluids with electrolytes cover the sweat. Eat a familiar meal 3 hours before competition and a carb-protein mix within 2 hours after. Supplements are the last one percent — food is the other ninety-nine.

title: Hydration plan
d: Track and Field hydration: start hydrated, drink to thirst plus plan, replace after.
definition: Track and Field hydration: start hydrated, drink to thirst plus plan, replace after.
description: Hydration for Track and Field: weigh before and after sessions to learn your sweat rate, drink on a schedule in long events, and replace sodium in heat. Losing two percent of body mass to dehydration measurably impairs skill and decisions. Practice the race-day drinking plan in training — never try anything new on competition day.

title: Recovery methods
d: Recover from Track and Field: sleep first, then easy movement, food, and stress control.
definition: Recover from Track and Field: sleep first, then easy movement, food, and stress control.
description: Recovery from Track and Field training ranks: sleep (8-9 hours for athletes) first, then light movement, then nutrition timing, then stress management. Ice baths and gadgets are minor compared to sleep. Track morning readiness — soreness, mood, resting heart rate — and adjust the day's load to it.

title: Sleep for athletes
d: Track and Field athletes need 8-9 hours: sleep is when training adaptations happen.
definition: Track and Field athletes need 8-9 hours: sleep is when training adaptations happen.
description: Sleep is the legal performance enhancer for Track and Field: growth hormone peaks in deep sleep, skills consolidate overnight, and reaction time degrades measurably with debt. Keep the room cool, dark, and screen-free; keep wake time consistent even on weekends. Naps of 20-30 minutes help; long late naps hurt night sleep.

title: Mental skills
d: Train the Track and Field mind: routines, self-talk, visualization, and pressure rehearsal.
definition: Train the Track and Field mind: routines, self-talk, visualization, and pressure rehearsal.
description: Mental training for Track and Field: a pre-performance routine that never changes, self-talk that is instructional not emotional, visualization of successful execution, and deliberate pressure practice. Confidence comes from preparation evidence — keep a log of good sessions to read before big events. Anxiety is normal; unmanaged anxiety is optional.

title: Season planning
d: Plan the Track and Field year: base, build, peak, and transition phases.
definition: Plan the Track and Field year: base, build, peak, and transition phases.
description: Season planning for Track and Field runs in phases: base (volume and technique), build (intensity and tactics), peak (sharpen for championships), transition (rest and play). One peak per season for most athletes; trying to peak year-round peaks never. Schedule deload weeks every 3-4 weeks — adaptation happens in recovery.

title: Tapering
d: Taper for Track and Field championships: cut volume 40-60%, keep intensity sharp.
definition: Taper for Track and Field championships: cut volume 40-60%, keep intensity sharp.
description: The Track and Field taper: 1-3 weeks out, cut training volume by 40 to 60 percent but keep some sharp intensity so the body stays awake. Sleep more, eat familiar food, trust the training. Most athletes taper too little and arrive flat, or train through and arrive tired — the taper is part of the program, not time off.

title: Youth development
d: Young Track and Field athletes: sample many sports, prioritize fun and fundamentals.
definition: Young Track and Field athletes: sample many sports, prioritize fun and fundamentals.
description: Youth Track and Field development: before age 14, multi-sport sampling beats early specialization for both skill and health. Keep sessions short, playful, and technique-rich; measure success in smiles and improvement, not trophies. Never year-round single-sport training before puberty — overuse injuries end more careers than opponents do.

title: Injury prevention
d: Prevent Track and Field injuries: warm up, strengthen the known weak links, manage load.
definition: Prevent Track and Field injuries: warm up, strengthen the known weak links, manage load.
description: Injury prevention in Track and Field targets the sport's known patterns: structured warm-ups (like FIFA 11+ style programs) cut injuries measurably, strength work protects joints, and load management — never spiking weekly volume more than about ten percent — prevents most overuse injuries. Report pain early; playing through sharp pain turns small problems into seasons lost.

title: Fitness testing
d: Test Track and Field fitness: repeat the same battery every 6-8 weeks.
definition: Test Track and Field fitness: repeat the same battery every 6-8 weeks.
description: Fitness testing for Track and Field: pick 4-6 tests covering speed, endurance, power, and sport skill, and repeat the identical battery every 6-8 weeks. Tests direct the program — train the weakest result. Record everything; athletes who test improve faster because the numbers make progress visible.

title: Return to play
d: Return to Track and Field after injury: criteria-based, not calendar-based.
definition: Return to Track and Field after injury: criteria-based, not calendar-based.
description: Return to Track and Field after injury follows criteria, not dates: full range of motion, strength symmetry, sport-specific movements pain-free, then controlled contact, then full training, then competition. Rushing back re-injures; the second injury is usually worse. Clearance from a clinician plus passing functional tests is the standard.

title: Pre-game routine
d: Track and Field pre-game: same timeline, same warm-up, same mindset every time.
definition: Track and Field pre-game: same timeline, same warm-up, same mindset every time.
description: The Track and Field pre-game routine: fixed timeline from arrival, dynamic warm-up progressing to sport speed, equipment check, tactical reminders, then quiet focus. Routines calm nerves by making the unfamiliar familiar. Rehearse the routine before minor events so it is automatic for major ones.

title: Video analysis
d: Study Track and Field film: your reps, opponents' tendencies, and elite models.
definition: Study Track and Field film: your reps, opponents' tendencies, and elite models.
description: Video analysis in Track and Field: review your own reps first (technique), then opponents (tendencies), then elite models (what great looks like). Keep clips short and specific — three clips with one fix each beats an hour of passive watching. Athletes who study film make better decisions under pressure.

title: Goal setting
d: Set Track and Field goals in three layers: outcome, performance, and process.
definition: Set Track and Field goals in three layers: outcome, performance, and process.
description: Goal setting for Track and Field: outcome goals (win the league) motivate, performance goals (improve first-touch success) direct, and process goals (today's drill focus) control the day. Write them down, review weekly, and keep process goals in the majority — athletes control effort and execution, not scoreboards.

title: Cross-training
d: Cross-train for Track and Field: swim, bike, or lift to build fitness without sport load.
definition: Cross-train for Track and Field: swim, bike, or lift to build fitness without sport load.
description: Cross-training for Track and Field keeps fitness growing while the sport-specific tissues rest: swimming for cardio without impact, cycling for legs without pounding, strength work for armor. One cross session weekly in season, more in the off-season. Variety also refreshes the mind — burnout ends more seasons than injuries do.

title: Equipment care
d: Track and Field gear lasts longer and performs better with basic maintenance.
definition: Track and Field gear lasts longer and performs better with basic maintenance.
description: Equipment care in Track and Field: clean it, dry it, store it right, and inspect it before every session. Worn gear causes injuries — dead shoes, frayed ropes, cracked helmets retire on schedule, not after failure. Keep a spare of anything that would end your day if it broke.

title: Travel competition
d: Travel for Track and Field events: control what you can — sleep, food, and warm-up.
definition: Travel for Track and Field events: control what you can — sleep, food, and warm-up.
description: Travel competition in Track and Field: arrive as early as the budget allows, bring familiar food, protect sleep across time zones, and scout the venue on arrival. Keep the pre-game routine identical to home — familiarity is calming. Pack backups of every critical item in carry-on.

title: Off-season
d: The Track and Field off-season: rest first, then rebuild the base and fix weaknesses.
definition: The Track and Field off-season: rest first, then rebuild the base and fix weaknesses.
description: The Track and Field off-season has two halves: complete rest for 2-4 weeks (mental and physical), then base rebuilding with high volume and low pressure. Fix the weakest link identified in testing, try a new sport for athleticism, and return to preseason hungry. Athletes who skip the off-season borrow from next year.
